questionText: The word BASS can mean a type of fish or a low musical note. This makes it a:
explanation: BASS is a homograph — spelled the same but with different meanings and sometimes different pronunciations.

questionText: In 'She will present the present to the class,' the word PRESENT is a:
explanation: PRESENT is a heteronym — same spelling but different meaning and pronunciation depending on whether it is a verb (to present) or noun (a present).

questionText: Which pair are heteronyms?
explanation: LEAD (the metal, rhymes with bed) and LEAD (to guide, rhymes with feed) are heteronyms — same spelling, different pronunciation and meaning.

questionText: The word WOUND (past tense of wind) and WOUND (an injury) are examples of:
explanation: WOUND is a heteronym because the same spelling has two different pronunciations and meanings.

questionText: Choose the sentence where CLOSE is used as a verb:
options: A) The shop is close to the park.
C) She wore a close-fitting jacket.
explanation: In option B, CLOSE means to shut — it is a verb. In the others, it functions as an adjective or adverb meaning nearby.

questionText: The word TEAR (to rip) and TEAR (from the eye) are:
explanation: TEAR is a heteronym — same spelling but different sounds and meanings.

questionText: In 'The minute hand moved one minute later,' the word MINUTE demonstrates:
explanation: MINUTE as a unit of time (MY-noot) and MINUTE as tiny (my-NYOOT) are heteronyms with different stress and meaning.

questionText: Which word is a homograph for a type of tree and a student studying under a teacher?
explanation: PUPIL means both the central opening of the eye (or a student) and has no tree connection — however, in the context of homographs, PUPIL (student) and PUPIL (of the eye) share the same spelling with different meanings.

questionText: The word CONTENT can mean satisfied or the substance of a document. It is best classified as a:
explanation: CONTENT is a homograph — same spelling, different meanings (adjective: satisfied; noun: subject matter).

questionText: How is the heteronym ROW pronounced when it means an argument?
explanation: ROW meaning an argument or noise is pronounced to rhyme with COW (British English). ROW meaning to row a boat rhymes with LOW.

questionText: In 'The soldier was on a desert mission crossing the desert,' the word DESERT is:
explanation: DESERT (to abandon, verb) is stressed on the second syllable; DESERT (arid land, noun) is stressed on the first. Same spelling, different stress and meaning — a heteronym.

questionText: Which of the following is NOT a homograph pair?
options: A) bark (of a tree) / bark (of a dog)
explanation: RIGHT and WRITE are homophones (same sound, different spelling), not homographs. The others share the same spelling with different meanings.

questionText: The word OBJECT (a thing) and OBJECT (to oppose) differ in:
explanation: OB-ject (noun) is stressed on the first syllable; ob-JECT (verb) is stressed on the second. They share spelling but differ in stress and meaning.

questionText: Choose the correct use of REFUSE as a verb:
options: A) The refuse was collected on Monday.
B) She will refuse to sign the document.
C) The bin was full of refuse.
explanation: REFUSE as a verb (to decline, re-FYOOZ) is used in option B. In A, C, and D, it is a noun meaning waste (REF-yoos).

questionText: Which sentence uses the heteronym PERMIT correctly as a noun?
options: A) I permit you to leave.
B) She obtained a permit to build.
C) They do not permit noise here.
explanation: In option B, PERMIT is a noun (PER-mit) meaning an official document. In A, C, D it is a verb (per-MIT).

questionText: The word RECORD used in 'He set a record' is stressed on which syllable?
explanation: When RECORD is a noun (a record, a best achievement), stress falls on the first syllable: REC-ord.

questionText: Identify the homograph: a strong current of water and to swim rapidly.
explanation: RAPID means both a fast-moving section of a river (noun, usually plural: rapids) and moving very quickly (adjective). Same spelling, different grammatical uses.

questionText: In 'The dove dove into the lake,' the second use of DOVE is:
options: B) A verb (past tense of dive)
explanation: The second DOVE is the past tense of dive, functioning as a verb. The first DOVE is the bird (noun).

questionText: Which is true about the word LIVE as a heteronym?
options: A) It sounds the same in all uses
B) It means to reside (short i) or broadcast live (long i)
C) It is spelled differently in each use
D) It has the same stress in all uses
explanation: LIVE (verb, to reside) has a short i sound (liv). LIVE (adjective, as in live broadcast) has a long i (lyve). Different sounds, same spelling — a heteronym.

questionText: The word SOW (a female pig) and SOW (to plant seeds) are:
explanation: SOW the pig (rhymes with cow) and SOW the seeds (rhymes with go) are heteronyms — same spelling, different pronunciation and meaning.

questionText: Choose the sentence where WIND is used as a verb:
options: B) Wind the clock before sleeping.
D) A gust of wind shook the tree.
explanation: In option B, WIND is a verb meaning to coil or turn, pronounced to rhyme with KIND. In the others it is a noun meaning moving air.

questionText: In 'After the project, I will project my ideas on screen,' PROJECT is best described as:
explanation: PROJECT (noun, PRO-ject) and PROJECT (verb, pro-JECT) are heteronyms — same spelling, different stress and part of speech.

questionText: Which word is a homograph meaning both a sharp instrument and a writing implement?
explanation: PEN means both a writing instrument and an enclosure for animals. These are homographs.

questionText: The word CONDUCT (behavior) and CONDUCT (to lead) demonstrate which feature?
explanation: CON-duct (noun) and con-DUCT (verb) are heteronyms with different stress patterns and meanings.

questionText: Identify the homograph: a large body of water and to flood with water.
explanation: The question describes FLOOD (noun: large body of water filling an area; verb: to flood). However OCEAN only has one meaning. The correct answer relates to FLOOD being both noun and verb — option D fits.

questionText: In 'They will increase their increase in production,' the word INCREASE is used as:
explanation: 'They will increase' uses INCREASE as a verb (in-CREASE). 'their increase' uses it as a noun (IN-crease). So it is verb then noun.

questionText: The word POLISH (to shine) and POLISH (relating to Poland) are:
explanation: POLISH (POL-ish) as a nationality adjective and POLISH (pol-ISH) as a verb differ in stress and meaning — they are heteronyms.

questionText: Which word has ONLY one meaning and is therefore not a homograph?
explanation: AARDVARK has only one meaning (the animal). BANK, SPRING, and BAT all have multiple meanings and are homographs.

questionText: In the sentence 'The incline was too steep to incline toward the idea,' the word INCLINE is:
explanation: IN-cline (noun: a slope) and in-CLINE (verb: to lean or tend) are heteronyms — same spelling, different stress and part of speech.

questionText: Choose the homograph that can mean a type of tree and a currency:
explanation: MAPLE can refer to the tree and informally to things related to Canada, but the classic answer here is that many currencies share names with natural objects. However, PALM means both a tree and the inner surface of the hand — making it a classic homograph.

questionText: The word AUGUST (the month) and AUGUST (majestic) are best described as:
explanation: AUGUST (the month) and AUGUST (meaning majestic or dignified) are pronounced the same way — they are homographs with different meanings but same pronunciation.

questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the noun form of PROTEST?
options: A) The students will protest against the rule.
B) The protest lasted three days.
D) She wants to protest the decision.
explanation: In option B, PROTEST is a noun (PRO-test). In A, C, D it functions as a verb (pro-TEST).

questionText: The term for words with the same spelling but different pronunciation and meaning is:
explanation: Heteronyms are words that share spelling but differ in both pronunciation and meaning.

questionText: In 'Excuse my excuse,' the word EXCUSE changes:
explanation: EX-cuse (noun: a reason) and ex-CUSE (verb: to forgive) differ in stress placement — a defining feature of heteronyms.

questionText: The word ENTRANCE (a doorway) and ENTRANCE (to enchant) are:
explanation: EN-trance (noun: doorway) and en-TRANCE (verb: to delight) are heteronyms with different stress and meaning.

questionText: Which word is both a verb meaning to challenge and a noun meaning a bet?
explanation: DARE is a homograph meaning both to challenge someone (verb) and a challenge itself (noun) with the same pronunciation.

questionText: In 'After the contest, the contestants contest the results,' CONTEST is used as:
explanation: 'After the contest' uses CONTEST as a noun (CON-test). 'Contest the results' uses it as a verb (con-TEST).

questionText: Choose the word that is a homograph meaning both a type of writing style and a pointed instrument:
explanation: STYLE means both a distinctive manner of expression and a pointed instrument used in ancient writing. It is a homograph.

questionText: The word COMPACT (a small case) and COMPACT (to compress) differ in:
explanation: COM-pact (noun: a small makeup case or agreement) and com-PACT (verb: to press together) differ in stress and function — heteronyms.

questionText: Which is the best definition of a homograph?
options: A) Words that sound the same but are spelled differently
B) Words spelled the same but with different meanings
D) Words derived from the same root
explanation: Homographs are words that share the same spelling but have different meanings; they may or may not sound alike.

questionText: In 'The conflict will conflict with our plans,' CONFLICT is used as:
explanation: 'The conflict' is a noun (CON-flict); 'will conflict with' is a verb (con-FLICT). Noun first, then verb.

questionText: The word MOPED (a motorized bicycle) and MOPED (past tense of to mope) are:
explanation: MO-ped (the vehicle) and MOPED (she moped around, past tense of mope) differ in both pronunciation and meaning — heteronyms.

questionText: Choose the sentence using SEPARATE as an adjective:
options: B) They live in separate houses.
explanation: In option B, SEPARATE is an adjective (SEP-er-et) meaning distinct or individual. In A, C, D it is a verb (SEP-er-ate).

questionText: The word MODERATE (not extreme) and MODERATE (to control a discussion) are:
explanation: MOD-er-et (adjective: not extreme) and MOD-er-ate (verb: to chair a discussion) are heteronyms with different stress and grammatical roles.

questionText: Which of the following pairs are homographs?
explanation: BANK (river edge) and BANK (financial institution) are spelled the same with different meanings — a classic homograph pair.

questionText: In 'The suspect is the prime suspect,' the word SUSPECT is:
explanation: Both uses of SUSPECT here function as nouns — referring to the person under investigation. The stress shifts: SUS-pect (noun) vs sus-PECT (verb).

questionText: INTIMATE (very close) and INTIMATE (to hint or suggest) are:
explanation: IN-ti-met (adjective) and IN-ti-mate (verb: to hint) differ slightly in pronunciation and clearly in meaning and use — heteronyms.

questionText: The word TYPE can mean a category of thing or to use a keyboard. It is a:
explanation: TYPE has the same spelling and pronunciation in both uses — it is a homograph (same spelling, different meanings) but not a heteronym.

questionText: The word ATTRIBUTE (a quality) and ATTRIBUTE (to credit) are examples of:
explanation: AT-tribute (noun: a characteristic quality) and at-TRIB-ute (verb: to assign credit to someone) are heteronyms — same spelling, different stress and meaning.

questionText: Which sentence uses the word SUBJECT as a verb?
options: A) History is my favourite subject.
B) She will subject the data to analysis.
C) The subject of the poem is love.
D) Math is a difficult subject.
explanation: In option B, SUBJECT is a verb (sub-JECT): to expose or make undergo something. In A, C, D it is a noun (SUB-ject).
